title: US Senator Pushes Bill to Grant Green Cards to Immigrants After Seven Years of Residency
excerpt: Senator Alex Padilla's legislation would update a 1929 immigration law, potentially opening a pathway for up to 8 million people including H-1B visa holders stuck in decades-long backlogs.
body:
• Senator Alex Padilla (D-CA) has reintroduced a bill that would grant Green Card eligibility to any immigrant who has lived in the U.S. continuously for at least seven years and has no criminal record.
  • The bill would update the Immigration Act of 1929's "registry" provision, whose cut-off date has been frozen at January 1, 1972 — more than 50 years ago.
  • Up to 8 million people could benefit, including DACA recipients, TPS holders and H-1B visa holders trapped in employment-based Green Card backlogs.
  • The bill faces long odds in a Republican-controlled Congress during an administration focused on immigration enforcement.

The Proposal

Senator Alex Padilla of California has reintroduced legislation that would fundamentally change how long-term residents of the United States can obtain permanent legal status. The bill — formally titled the "Renewing Immigration Provisions of the Immigration Act of 1929" — would create a rolling registry date, allowing any immigrant who has lived in the country continuously for at least seven years and is of good moral character to apply for a Green Card.

Under current law, the registry statute's cut-off date is January 1, 1972. That means only immigrants who can prove continuous residence since before that date — more than 54 years ago — are eligible. Padilla's bill would eliminate the fixed date in favour of a seven-year rolling window.

Who Would Benefit

The legislation could open a pathway for up to 8 million people, according to estimates from FWD.us, an immigration advocacy group. The beneficiaries would span a wide range of immigration statuses: DACA recipients, Temporary Protected Status holders, children of long-term visa holders who face aging out of the system, essential workers and — critically for the Indian diaspora — highly skilled H-1B visa holders who have been waiting years or decades for employment-based Green Cards.

Indian nationals face the longest Green Card wait times of any nationality due to per-country caps. The employment-based Green Card backlog for Indians has been estimated at over 100 years for some categories, creating a limbo in which workers remain legally employed but unable to change jobs freely, start businesses or plan long-term.

"America's outdated immigration system is hurting countless people and holding back our country and our economy."

— Senator Alex Padilla (D-CA)

The Economic Argument

Proponents argue the bill would deliver a substantial economic boost. According to FWD.us, if the undocumented individuals covered by the legislation became citizens, they would contribute approximately $121 billion to the U.S. economy annually and about $35 billion in taxes. The estimate does not include the economic gains from unlocking mobility for skilled workers currently constrained by visa restrictions.

Political Reality

The bill faces steep odds. Republicans control both chambers of Congress, and immigration proposals that expand pathways to legal status have found little traction in the current political environment. The Trump administration's focus on enforcement — including accelerated deportation proceedings and restrictions on student visas — runs counter to the bill's expansive approach.

Previous versions of the legislation, co-sponsored by senators including Dick Durbin, Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren, did not advance to a vote. But for immigration advocates and the millions of Indian-origin workers navigating the system, the bill keeps the conversation alive about structural reform that both parties have avoided for decades.
nri_angle: Hundreds of thousands of Indian-origin H-1B holders face Green Card wait times exceeding 100 years under the current system — this bill could offer a dramatic shortcut.
